public_payload.normalized_proposition: AI is not replacing software engineers; they are being laid off because AI tooling is so expensive.

statement.excerpt: Software engineers aren’t being replaced — they’re being laid off because the software that’s meant to replace them is too expensive, while in practice not replacing anybody at all.
statement.document_title: The AI Industry Is Lying To You

from_speaker: being laid off because the software that’s meant to replace them is too expensive
our_interpretation: The ordinary reading asserts budget crowd-out: AI software costs cause engineering layoffs, while AI does not actually take over the eliminated work.
Replacement includes AI taking over enough work to eliminate an engineering position; it does not require autonomous performance of every engineering task.
I examine the contemporary layoff episode from 2025 through the post date. This is an evaluator-defined window because the speaker supplies no dates.
Spending to develop AI products or build data centers is not automatically spending on software intended to replace engineers.
Employer statements about expected efficiency establish a stated motive, not verified task replacement.
criteria.support_condition: Representative budget and work-allocation records show that AI software spending caused engineering job cuts and that AI did not take over the eliminated work, with plausible competing causes addressed.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Verified cases show AI actually taking over eliminated software-engineering work, contradicting the no-replacement assertion, or credible causal evidence rejects AI software costs as the explanation for the layoffs described.

evidence.explanation: Atlassian explicitly links workforce reductions to financing investment, which is consistent with part of the proposed mechanism. Its statement covers broader investment and workforce changes, not a demonstrated engineering-tool bill or proof that eliminated engineering work remained unautomated.

The report gives Block's expected-efficiency explanation, an alternative to layoffs caused solely by expensive tools. It does not independently verify completed replacement of software engineers; secondary reporting is used because the primary letter was inaccessible to read_page.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Corroborated records linking engineering layoffs to AI tooling costs, together with evidence showing whether AI, remaining staff, contractors or discontinued projects absorbed the eliminated work.
